# Preface {.unnumbered}

A practical guide to getting work done on **MedicineBow**, the University of Wyoming's
high-performance computing (HPC) cluster, run by the **Advanced Research Computing Center
(ARCC)**.

It is written for people joining the **ASCEND** engine and its **ARID** program, and
assumes you are comfortable on a computer but have never used a shared supercomputer. Each
chapter explains *why* before *how*.

## Why this book exists

The official documentation — the [ARCC wiki](https://pages.arcc.uwyo.edu/arcc-wiki/main/) —
is good but has gaps and is in places out of date. The content here was written while
onboarding on the live cluster and cross-checked against the running system in July 2026.
Where the docs and the machine disagree, this book follows the machine and notes the
conflict.

::: {.callout-note}
## This is not an official ARCC document
It's a community onboarding guide. It can drift out of date, and ARCC can change
policy at any time. When in doubt, the
[official wiki](https://pages.arcc.uwyo.edu/arcc-wiki/main/) and
`arcc-help@uwyo.edu` are authoritative. Corrections are very welcome.
:::

## Quick orientation

1. **Request your account by emailing Virginia Iglesias** (<virginia@innosphere.org>), who
   coordinates ASCEND/ARID access. (See @sec-account.)
2. **Nothing on the cluster is backed up.** Not home, not project, not scratch. There
   are snapshots, but they live on the same array. (See @sec-storage.)
3. **Never run real computation on a login node.** Log in, then hand work to the
   scheduler (Slurm) or grab an interactive session. (See @sec-why-scheduler.)
4. **Every job must name your project account** with `--account=<project>`. (See
   @sec-anatomy.)
5. **The partition (hardware pool) and QOS (quality-of-service tier) you choose decide how long you wait and how big you can go.**
   Short test runs and long simulations belong in different queues (@sec-partitions,
   @sec-queue-times).

## How the book is organized

The chapters run in the order you'll need them:

1. **Getting started on the cluster** — what an HPC cluster is, how to request an account, and
   first login through the portal and SSH keys.
2. **Linux essentials** — the minimum shell you need: moving around, editing files, and keeping
   work alive across a dropped connection with `tmux`.
3. **Storage and moving data** — the three filesystems (and the fact that nothing is backed
   up), plus Globus, `rsync`, and `rclone` for transfers.
4. **Software: modules, conda, and containers** — loading software with Lmod, using conda
   without filling your home directory, and running containers with Apptainer.
5. **Running jobs with Slurm** — why a scheduler exists, the anatomy of a batch job, and asking
   for the right resources.
6. **Partitions, QOS, and queue times** — which hardware and service tier to choose, measured
   wait times, and how job priority is actually computed here.
7. **Monitoring, arrays, and interactive jobs** — watching and diagnosing jobs, job arrays,
   interactive and GPU sessions, and the parallelism ladder.
8. **Preemption, checkpointing, and failures** — surviving the condo model (shared, investor-owned hardware that can reclaim your job) and walltime limits,
   and reading the wreckage when a job fails.
9. **Agentic coding with Claude** — using an AI coding agent for cluster work, and the two
   rules that matter: verify its output, and mind what data you send.
10. **Reference** — a command cheat sheet, a symptom-to-fix troubleshooting index, and a
    glossary.
